alerts.title: Rising creatinine and declining eGFR on TDF
alerts.message: TDF is associated with renal toxicity including proximal tubular dysfunction and declining eGFR. This patient's creatinine has progressively risen from 0.9 mg/dL (2020) to 1.4 mg/dL (2026), with eGFR now 52 mL/min/1.73m². Urinalysis shows protein 1+ and trace glucose, consistent with proximal tubular damage. Evidence for drug attribution: steady creatinine rise temporally tracks 3 years of TDF exposure, and proteinuria plus glucosuria are hallmark features of TDF tubulopathy. Evidence against: no peripheral oedema, stable weight, and no costovertebral angle tenderness; alternative causes such as occasional ibuprofen use (2-3 times weekly for 6 months) or subclinical infection should also be evaluated. The progressive trend is concerning even though the latest value alone may appear modest.

evidence.recommended_action: Evaluate renal function trends and consider switching TDF to TAF or ABC. Assess for alternative causes of renal decline including NSAID-related nephropathy. Refer for nephrology evaluation if indicated.

alerts.title: No clinician assessment or plan documented
alerts.message: Guidelines require systematic screening and management of adverse drug reactions and comorbidities at each clinical visit. Today's encounter has no documented assessment or plan despite abnormal renal indices (creatinine 1.4, eGFR 52, proteinuria) and a 6-year progressive creatinine trend. The patient also reports mild fatigue and regular ibuprofen use. Without a plan, the renal abnormalities and potential TDF toxicity will go unaddressed. The clinician should document assessment, order appropriate follow-up labs, and outline management steps.

evidence.recommended_action: Document clinical assessment and management plan addressing renal function decline, proteinuria, ongoing TDF safety, and ibuprofen use. Order repeat renal panel and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio.

alerts.title: Ibuprofen use with renal impairment on TDF
alerts.message: The patient takes ibuprofen 400 mg 2-3 times weekly for headaches over 6 months. With eGFR at 52 mL/min/1.73m² and evidence of TDF-associated renal toxicity (proteinuria, rising creatinine), concurrent NSAID use compounds risk of further kidney injury. Guidelines note that patients with uncontrolled comorbidities may suffer complications including chronic kidney disease. While occasional ibuprofen may be acceptable with normal renal function, this patient's compromised eGFR and active proteinuria make regular NSAID use hazardous. Alternative analgesics such as paracetamol should be considered for headache management.

evidence.recommended_action: Counsel patient to reduce or discontinue ibuprofen given renal impairment. Recommend paracetamol for headache relief. Address underlying causes of recurrent headaches including work-related stress.

alerts.title: Monitoring gaps: renal and metabolic labs overdue
alerts.message: Guidelines list hyperglycemia/diabetes and abnormal weight gain as adverse events to screen for, particularly with DTG-containing regimens. This patient's urinalysis shows trace glucose, but no fasting blood glucose or HbA1c is documented. Additionally, no urine protein-to-creatinine ratio has been ordered to quantify the proteinuria detected on dipstick. Given the declining eGFR and TDF exposure, a quantitative protein assessment is essential to differentiate TDF tubulopathy from other renal pathology. No lipid panel is documented despite DTG being associated with metabolic changes. These monitoring gaps should be addressed in the plan.

evidence.recommended_action: Order fasting blood glucose or HbA1c, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, and lipid panel to complete safety monitoring for TDF/DTG regimen.
